Welcome to Redeemer Covenant

A place to encounter grace, truth, and community

We are a confessional Baptist church in the Reformed tradition, holding to the Second London Baptist Confession of Faith (1689) as our subordinate doctrinal standard. We have been gathering in Arlington since 2014 — committed to expository preaching, covenantal worship, and the historic Baptist faith.

We are also a member church of the Fellowship of Independent Reformed Evangelicals (FIRE) — a network of like-minded confessional churches.

Our Identity

About Redeemer Covenant

Reformed Baptist. Confessional. Welcoming. Rooted in Arlington, Ohio since 2014.

Our Story

Who We Are

Redeemer Covenant Church is a Reformed Baptist congregation in Arlington, Ohio — a community of people who have been transformed by God's sovereign grace and are committed to worshiping Him according to His Word.

We have been gathering in Arlington since 2014, and are in fellowship with the Fellowship of Independent Reformed Evangelicals (FIRE) — a network of like-minded Reformed Baptist churches.

Our aim is simple: to glorify God and enjoy Him forever through faith in the person and work of Jesus Christ — seeking always to reform our worship and our theology according to the Scriptures alone.

2014 — Founded

Redeemer Covenant Church is constituted in Arlington, Ohio.

FIRE Fellowship

Joined the Fellowship of Independent Reformed Evangelicals, connecting with sister churches across the region.

Today — Growing

A warm, close-knit congregation committed to expository preaching, robust fellowship, and discipleship.

Our Doctrine

What We Believe

We are a confessionally Reformed Baptist church. That means we hold to the historic doctrines of Scripture — summarized beautifully in the 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith.

The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith

"We regard the Second London Confession of Faith of 1689 as an excellent, though not inspired, expression of the teaching of those Holy Scriptures by which all confessions are to be measured."

Read Our Full Doctrine Page →

Scripture Alone

The Holy Bible is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience.

Grace Alone, Faith Alone

Sinners are justified before God by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone — not by any works or merit of our own.

God's Sovereign Grace

Salvation is entirely God's work from beginning to end — He elects, calls, regenerates, justifies, and glorifies His people according to His own sovereign will.

The Church & Ordinances

We practice believer's baptism by immersion and observe the Lord's Supper regularly as a memorial of Christ's death and a pledge of His return.

Regulative Principle of Worship

We worship God only as He has commanded in His Word — His glory, not our preferences, directs the form and content of our corporate worship.

Elder-Led Congregationalism

The local church is governed by a plurality of elders (pastors), accountable to the congregation, with deacons serving in practical ministry.

About · Our Worship

Integrated Worship

God calls all people — young and old, new believers and seasoned saints — to worship Him together in one assembly.

What Is Integrated Worship?

One Assembly Before God

At Redeemer Covenant Church, we do not separate children from the congregation during Lord's Day worship. We gather as one body — the very young and the very old, new converts and longtime believers — to hear the Word of God preached, to sing His praises, and to call upon His name together.

This practice flows from a conviction that corporate worship is not a service designed for a particular demographic. It is the gathered people of God — in all their variety — responding to His call. The pew is a place for every person who belongs to Christ, regardless of age.

"Gather the people — men, women, and little ones"

— Deuteronomy 31:12. God has always summoned His people to assemble together. The young and the old stand before Him in the same moment, hearing the same Word, singing the same praises.

The Foundation

The Primacy of Preaching

God has appointed preaching as His ordinary means of saving and sanctifying His people. The Lord's Day gathering is the central act of the Christian week — not a program to be customized by age group, but the event itself. The sermon is not background noise while children are elsewhere. It is what we are here for, and every person present is under its address.

A Word to Visitors

You Are Welcome As You Are

If you are visiting with young children who have never sat through a full service, please know that our congregation is patient and warm. We have a back area for those who need a few minutes to settle. The first few Sundays may feel unfamiliar — but we have watched many people grow into this practice and come to treasure it.

Why We Worship This Way

The Reasons Behind the Practice

God calls all people to worship

The summons of God in Scripture does not come to adults only. "Let everything that has breath praise the Lord" (Ps. 150:6). Corporate worship is the response of the whole people of God — in every season of life — to His gracious call. Age does not disqualify; it diversifies the assembly.

Conscience is trained by participation

Reverence is not merely taught — it is caught. A child who sits through the preaching of the Word, who hears the congregation sing with conviction, who watches older believers bow in prayer, is having their conscience formed toward what is holy. This formation happens slowly, over years, and it is irreplaceable.

The young learn from the old; the old are renewed by the young

When the full breadth of the congregation worships side by side, something is given and received that cannot be manufactured in age-segregated settings. The seasoned believer models endurance; the young child embodies the openness the Lord commended. Both are enriched by the presence of the other.

Habits of worship are a gift for life

We have seen children who once squirmed through sermons grow into teenagers who open their Bibles and follow along, and then into young adults who regard the Lord's Day as the best day of the week. The habits of reverence formed early are among the most durable gifts the church can give to the next generation.

Questions about our worship service?

We are happy to talk through what a Sunday looks like before you visit — just reach out.

Teaching · Doctrine

Confessions & Catechisms

How historic summaries of Scripture serve the church — and why the Bible always stands above them.

Scripture First, Always

The Word Above All

Redeemer Covenant Church is a confessional church. We hold to the Second London Baptist Confession of Faith (1689) as our subordinate standard — meaning it stands under Scripture, not alongside it. Where the Confession speaks, we receive it as a wise guide. Where Scripture corrects it, Scripture wins.

This is not a contradiction. Confessing that Scripture is supreme does not mean every Christian must derive every doctrine from scratch in every generation. God has been gracious to His church across centuries, and the confessions faithful men produced are gifts — tested by time, refined by controversy, and handed down for our benefit.

What does "subordinate standard" mean?

It means the Confession is a tool in service of Scripture — not a replacement for it. We subscribe to the 1689 because we believe it accurately summarizes what the Bible teaches, and for no other reason. If it erred, we would correct it by the Word.

Our Confession

The 1689 London Baptist Confession

The 2nd London Baptist Confession (1689) is the primary doctrinal standard of Redeemer Covenant Church. Drawn from the Westminster Confession and the Savoy Declaration, it represents the mature Reformed theology of our Particular Baptist forebears — men who were willing to suffer for what they believed Scripture taught.

Read the 1689 Confession →

Other Confessional Documents

AD 1646
First London Baptist Confession
The earlier confession of the Particular Baptists — a witness to their Reformed identity from the beginning.
AD 1561
Belgic Confession
One of the Three Forms of Unity — a beautiful statement of Reformed theology from the Dutch Reformation.
AD 1563
Heidelberg Catechism
The warmest of the Reformed catechisms — guilt, grace, and gratitude. Widely used for family instruction.
For Memorization & Formation

Catechisms

Catechisms are question-and-answer summaries of Christian doctrine — tools for buttressing Scripture memorization with doctrinal confession, and for training children (and adults) in the faith. They do not replace Bible reading; they make Bible reading more fruitful.

Baptist Catechism — Keach's (1693)

The classic catechism for Reformed Baptist churches. 114 questions covering Christian doctrine in a form suitable for children and adults alike. The natural companion to the 1689 Confession for family worship.

Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647)

107 questions beginning with "What is the chief end of man?" Memorized by generations of Reformed Christians. Its language has shaped the devotional vocabulary of the church for nearly four centuries.

New City Catechism

A modern, accessible 52-question catechism drawing on historic sources. Suitable for young children beginning their doctrinal instruction, with memory verses and accompanying devotionals for each question.

Heidelberg Catechism (1563)

Organized around three themes — guilt, grace, and gratitude. Among the most beloved of all Reformed catechisms, with a warmth and pastoral depth that makes it suitable for every season of the Christian life.

Teaching · Reformed Theology

Exploring Reformed Theology

A guide to the great biblical doctrines recovered by the Reformation — still alive, still necessary, still glorious.

Why Reformed Theology?

Not a Brand — A Recovery

The word "Reformed" describes a tradition, not a tribal identity. It refers to the theological recovery — begun in the 16th century and continuing today — of doctrines that Scripture plainly teaches but that had been obscured: the sovereignty of God in salvation, the grace of election, the sufficiency of Christ's atonement, the necessity of new birth, and the freedom of a conscience bound to God's Word alone.

These are not academic curiosities. They are the load-bearing walls of the Christian faith. The topics below offer brief introductions to the core categories of Reformed theology as we hold and practice them at Redeemer Covenant Church.

01
Covenant Theology

God has always related to His people through covenants. Covenant theology traces these covenants from Eden through Abraham, Moses, and David, and shows how they all find their fulfillment in the new covenant sealed by the blood of Christ.

Gen. 15 · Jer. 31:31–34 · Heb. 8–10
Read more →
02
The Doctrines of Grace

Sometimes called the "five points of Calvinism," the Doctrines of Grace describe what the Bible teaches about human sinfulness and God's sovereign mercy: Total Depravity, Unconditional Election, Definite Atonement, Irresistible Grace, and Perseverance of the Saints.

John 6:37–44 · Eph. 1:3–14 · Rom. 8:28–39
Read more →
03
The Free Offer of the Gospel

God's sovereign election does not cancel the genuine, well-meant offer of the gospel to every sinner without exception. We preach Christ freely to all — "Come to me, all who are weary" — confident that every soul who hears has a genuine and sincere invitation to come.

Matt. 11:28 · Isa. 55:1 · Rev. 22:17
Read more →
04
Reformed Worship

The Regulative Principle holds that God is to be worshipped only as He has commanded in Scripture — not as we might imagine or devise. This shapes every element of our Lord's Day service: reading and preaching of the Word, prayer, congregational psalm and hymn singing, and the sacraments.

Lev. 10:1–3 · Deut. 12:32 · Col. 3:16
Read more →
05
The Ordinary Means of Grace

God has appointed ordinary means through which He works saving and sanctifying grace: the Word preached and read, the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper, and prayer. "Ordinary" not because they are unimportant, but because they are the regular, appointed channels of His grace — to be used diligently.

Rom. 10:17 · 1 Cor. 11:23–26 · James 5:16
Read more →
06
The Reformation & Baptist History

We are what Baptists used to be. The Particular Baptists of 17th-century England were Reformed in theology, covenantal in their reading of Scripture, and willing to suffer for their convictions. Understanding their history helps us understand who we are and why these doctrines matter today.

Acts 20:27 · 2 Tim. 1:13–14 · Jude 3
Read more →

Questions about Reformed theology?

We would love to talk through any of these topics with you in person. Our elders are available to meet.
